transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, what brings me in today is... I just keep forgetting things that I really shouldn’t. Important things, you know? 

Like, I'll completely miss my heart follow-up appointments, or I'll forget to call the clinic back when I'm supposed to. And it's not just the medical stuff. I'll go to start a repair job around the house and realize I showed up without the right tools for it. It's just happening a lot lately, and I wanted to get it checked out.
When did you first notice this problem with forgetting things starting to happen? Was it sudden, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?

Well, it hasn't been sudden, really. It's been causing real trouble for about... I'd say a year and two months now. That's when I had a cardiac scare, and I had to cut way back on all my walking and the house projects. Those things used to keep me settled, I guess. Since I had to slow down, the forgetting just seems to have gotten worse.

Besides forgetting things, have you noticed any other changes in how your mind works? For example, do you have trouble finding the right words, or difficulty with tasks that require planning or organizing?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I don't have any trouble finding the right words when I'm talking to folks. And as for planning... well, I know how to organize a repair job just fine. I've been doing them my whole life. It's just that I'll walk all the way out there and realize I didn't bring the tools I actually needed. So, no, I think my mind works okay for figuring things out and talking. It's really just the forgetting part.

Since your heart scare about a year ago, have you noticed that you're feeling down or depressed? Or have activities that you used to enjoy—like those house projects and walks—stopped being enjoyable even when you could do them?

No, I haven't felt down or depressed. I mean, it's a little frustrating having to take it easy, but I still enjoy my projects just as much as I always did. I still want to do them. It's just... well, like I said, I get out there and realize I don't have the right wrench or whatever. But the enjoyment is definitely still there when I can actually get to work. So, no, nothing like that.
When you think back to things that happened in the past—say, events from last month or last year—do you have trouble recalling those memories, or is your memory for past events pretty much normal?

No, I don't have any trouble with that. Things from last month or last year... I remember all that just fine. 

It's really just the day-to-day stuff, like I said, forgetting my tools and whatnot. But if you ask me about something that happened a while back, I'd say my memory for that is pretty much normal.

When you plan to do something—like remembering to take a medication at a certain time, or remembering that you need to pick something up from the store—do you find yourself forgetting those plans even though you knew about them when you made them?

No, I don't really have a problem with that. If I need to take my pills, I remember to take them. And if I plan to go to the store for something, I make sure I get it. 

Like I was saying, it's more about walking out to the yard and forgetting which tool I just had in my hand or what I went out there for in that exact second. But as far as remembering plans I made or things I need to do later in the day... no, I keep track of those just fine.

When you're working on one of your house projects and you're focused on it, do you find it hard to concentrate or stay on task? Or do you sometimes lose track of what you're doing while you're actually in the middle of doing it?

Well, it's not just the house projects. It's... if I sit down to play cards with the guys, or I'm at a planning meeting for the Fix-It Friends, I really mean to pay close attention. But after a little while, my mind just kind of slides off. I'll suddenly realize I haven't been listening and I missed half of what was said. So, yeah, staying focused on one thing for very long is definitely hard for me.

When you forget something like where you put your tools or what you went out to do, is it because you weren't really paying attention when you were doing it or setting it down? Or is it that you were paying attention at the time, but then the memory just slipped away?

I'm... I'm really not sure how to answer that. I haven't really thought about it that way before. 

I mean, when I set a tool down, I feel like I know what I'm doing right in that exact moment. But then I turn around a minute later and it's just gone from my head. I couldn't tell you for sure if I just wasn't paying close enough attention when I let go of it, or if the memory just slipped away right after. I just know I end up standing there scratching my head, wondering where I put the darn thing.

Around the time of your cardiac scare about a year ago, did you experience any head injury, fall, or loss of consciousness? Or did you have a stroke or any other neurological event that the doctors mentioned?

No, nothing like that. I didn't fall or hit my head, and I definitely didn't pass out. The doctors never mentioned anything about a stroke or any kind of... neurological thing. It was just the heart scare, plain and simple.

When you're trying hard to remember something—like if I asked you right now to tell me what tools you used on a project last week, or what you had for lunch yesterday—can you usually bring that information back to mind if you really concentrate on it?

I guess... I'm not really sure. I haven't really tested it out like that. If I forget what tool I used, I usually just go look out in the garage instead of standing there trying to force my brain to remember it. So I couldn't tell you for sure if concentrating really hard brings it back or not.

If I were to ask you right now to describe in detail what you did this morning—like what you ate for breakfast, what clothes you wore, who you talked to—could you recall those details pretty clearly, or would those things be fuzzy or hard to remember?

I could tell you that pretty clearly. I had a bowl of oatmeal and some coffee, threw on my blue jeans and a flannel shirt. Talked to my wife for a bit before she headed out. That stuff isn't fuzzy at all. It's just the little things, like where I set my wrench down five minutes ago, that give me trouble. But what I actually did this morning? Yeah, I remember that fine.
After your heart scare, did the doctors find anything else going on—like problems with your blood sugar, thyroid, or blood pressure? Or did they start you on any new medications around that time?

No, they didn't find anything else. They ran plenty of blood work, but... my blood sugar and thyroid were fine, and my blood pressure is normal. And they didn't start me on any new pills or anything like that after it happened. It was really just the heart issue, nothing else.

Can you tell me today's date, what day of the week it is, and where we are right now? And do you generally know those things throughout the day, or do you sometimes get confused about what day or time it is?

Well, today's Thursday, October 12th, and we're at your clinic. I don't really get confused about that kind of stuff. I might have to glance at a calendar sometimes to remember the exact date, but I always know what day of the week it is and where I am. I never feel lost or confused about the time.
Earlier in our conversation, I asked you about your heart scare. Can you tell me what year that happened, or roughly how long ago it was?

Well, I'm not exactly sure what year it was, to be honest. It's been a little while. I'd probably have to go look at my paperwork at home to give you the exact date or how many years it's been. I just know it happened, but the specific year kind of escapes me right now.

You mentioned you remember to take your pills and keep track of plans. But when you're supposed to do something at a specific time—like remember to call your doctor back at 2 PM, or remember that you have an appointment next Tuesday—do you actually remember those things when the time comes, or do you forget them even though you knew about them beforehand?

Well, honestly, that's exactly what brings me in. I actually do forget them when the time comes. I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn't. 

Like, I'll completely miss my heart follow-up appointments, or I'll forget to call the clinic back when I'm supposed to. It just goes right out of my head. And it's everyday stuff, too... like, I'll head out to do a repair job, and I'll show up without the right tools, even though I knew perfectly well what I needed before I walked out the door. So, yeah, even if I know about it ahead of time, I still end up forgetting.

If I gave you three words right now—let's say 'apple,' 'table,' and 'blue'—and asked you to remember them, do you think you could hold those three words in your mind and tell them back to me in a few minutes?

Well... apple, table, blue. I mean, I have them in my head right now. But if we keep talking for a few minutes and you ask me again? I'm honestly not sure. 

I'd like to think I could remember just three words, but with the way I've been forgetting my appointments and leaving my tools behind, I might end up dropping one of them by the time you ask. I guess we can try it and see what happens, but I wouldn't make any promises.

Let me ask you this: when you're having a conversation with someone and they're talking to you, can you usually follow along and remember what they just said a few sentences back? Or do you find that you lose track of what the conversation was about?

Well, it depends. If it's a short conversation, I'm usually okay. But if it goes on for a bit... yeah, I definitely lose track. Like, I can sit down at the bridge table, or, you know, we have these planning meetings for my Fix-It Friends group. And I go in fully meaning to pay close attention. But after a little while, my mind just kind of... slides off. And then I suddenly realize I've missed half of what was just said. So, yeah, I do have trouble following along if it's more than just a quick chat.
A few minutes ago, I gave you three words to remember: apple, table, and blue. Can you tell me those three words back to me now?

Apple... table... and... 

See, this is exactly what I was talking about. I know there was a third one. Apple, table... was it a color? I want to say red, but that doesn't feel right. 

No, I'm sorry, I've lost the last one. Just apple and table.
